sources.note: Only about Warembori, not Pauwi: 'Stress is normally assigned to the penultimate syllable of a word or compound' (section 2.2, p. 7-8), with exceptions for nasal-final roots, all-identical vowels (final stress) and 'heavy' consonants. Pauwi appears only in the bibliography (Van der Aa 1885); section 1.1 speaks of 'a no-longer extant language which was related to Yoke' as a source of Warembori vocabulary.

sources.citation: Wikipedia articles 'Yoke language' and 'Lower Mamberamo languages' (read 2026-09-17).
sources.note: No stress information. The Yoke article states that the 19th-century 'Pauwi' wordlist collected by Robidé van der Aa at Lake Rombebai 'is transparently Yoke' and lists Pauwi as an alternative designation of Yoke; its Yoke phonology section has no prosody.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: Checklist. Preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists. Pacific Linguistics B-31. Canberra: ANU. Entry 152 'PAUWI ISOLATE', pp. 52-53.
sources.note: Nothing. 'It is doubtful whether the language is still spoken. When first recorded, Pauwi was spoken by an estimated 100 people living in a village on the Mamberamo River at about 25 kilometers from the sea... The two short wordlists on hand share a few probable cognates with Warenbori, Tarunggare, Baropasi, Kwerba and the Tor languages... Sources: Robidé van der Aa 1885 (Wl); Moszkowski 1911 (N); Anonymous 1913 (Wl).' No Pauwi wordlist reproduced.

sources.citation: Anonymous [Max Moszkowski]. 1913. Wörterverzeichnisse von Papua-Sprachen aus Holländisch-Neuguinea. Anthropos 8: 254-259 (Analecta et Additamenta).
sources.note: No statement. Four-column wordlist (Borumessu, Koassa, Pauwi, Südfluss) plus a Pauwi supplement on p. 259; the Pauwi forms carry acute accents on one syllable (passára 'Schädel', pamabúna 'Bart', péro 'Schwein', suába 'Kasuar', oschénu 'eins', biméssi 'drei', kinguéri 'wir zwei', bimbájo, tabáko), which is the German ethnographers' convention for the stressed syllable, but the text never says so and gives no rule; the only remark is 'Pauwi (anscheinend mit Nufoor Elementen gemischt)' (p. 254).

sources.citation: Moszkowski, Max. 1911. Die Völkerstämme am Mamberamo in Holländisch-Neuguinea und auf den vorgelagerten Inseln. Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 43: 315-346.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic lecture; no wordlist. p. 318 only says the coastal languages are Malayo-Polynesian and names Numfor/Windessi; p. 321-322 says the Pauwi people count only to five; p. 332 says the village Pauwi (25 km upstream) was half interior 'Pauwi' people and half coastal Bossumassin, children speaking the mother's language.

sources.citation: Robidé van der Aa, P. J. B. C. 1885. Reizen van D. F. van Braam Morris naar de Noordkust van Nederlandsch Nieuw-Guinea. Eerste vaart op de Amberno- of Rochussen-rivier. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde van Nederlandsch-Indië 34: 73-114; Bijlage 'Woordenlijstje der taal van Pauwi (benedenloop der Rochussen-Rivier)', pp. 111-114.
sources.note: Nothing. About 60 words plus numerals ('kait pasari' one, 'kait pari' two...) taken from Mr Kerkhove's 1884 journal; the words are printed in italics without accent marks (p. 114 checked as a page image); Van der Aa's remarks (pp. 111-113) concern only the numerals and possible Mafoor/Numfor affinities.
